name: Canadian national general contractor (commercial, institutional and industrial buildings)
modelled_on: Bird Construction Inc. (TSX: BDT), from its 2019-2022 annual results releases and company web pages
summary: The organisation is a Canadian general contractor that builds hospitals, schools, universities, offices, warehouses, plants and other non-residential buildings for public institutions, private owners and P3 consortia. It earns money by winning contracts and building them for more than they cost: stipulated price (lump-sum) bids for public tenders, construction management and design-build contracts for a fee, and the design-build role in public-private partnerships. Most of the work, such as mechanical, electrical, steel and envelope, is subcontracted to trade contractors that the company prequalifies, hires and pays; its own union crews self-perform structural concrete, carpentry and general labour using company cranes, formwork and yards. Owners pay monthly against certified progress draws, and Ontario's Construction Act sets prompt payment deadlines, a 10% holdback and lien rights that run down to every subcontractor. The head office is in Ontario and regional offices in Western and Atlantic Canada run about 220 active projects at a time with salaried project managers, superintendents and engineers. Central business development, finance, safety, supply chain, HR, IT and legal departments support the regions, and the company is listed on the TSX and reports quarterly.

process_map.name: Set the strategic plan
process_map.description: The executive team reviews markets, backlog, margins and risk appetite each year and sets target sectors, regions, delivery models and growth or acquisition plans. Board approval is required. The hard part is balancing fixed-price exposure against collaborative contracts.

evidence.note: Standard governance of a listed contractor.

process_map.name: Report to and support the board
process_map.description: Management prepares quarterly board and committee packs on results, backlog, safety, major project risks and dividends, and records board decisions. Audit and risk committees review the large fixed-price projects and claims.

evidence.note: Standard governance of a TSX-listed company.

process_map.name: Approve large bids and proposals
process_map.description: Bids above a threshold (for example $25M, or any P3 or unusual contract terms) go to an executive risk review of cost, fee, contingency, contract terms and resourcing before submission. Reviews happen on short notice in the last days before bid close.

evidence.note: Common practice of listed builders after fixed-price losses; threshold is an estimate.

process_map.name: Review the project portfolio each month
process_map.description: Executives and regional vice-presidents review each region's cost forecasts, margin fade, claims, safety statistics and cash, and agree corrective actions on troubled projects. Results feed the quarterly outlook.

evidence.note: Typical monthly operations review in contractors.

process_map.name: Track opportunities and decide go or no-go
process_map.description: Business development and estimating screen public tenders on bid portals and private leads, record them in the CRM and decide whether to pursue based on fit, competition, workload, bonding and risk. Most invitations are declined; picking the right ones sets the hit rate.

evidence.note: Practice of commercial-institutional builders; volumes estimated.

process_map.name: Respond to owner prequalification requests
process_map.description: Public owners and P3 sponsors shortlist contractors through RFQs. Proposal coordinators assemble experience, key staff resumes, safety statistics, COR status, financial capacity and surety letters into a scored submission.

evidence.note: Common public procurement practice in Canada.

process_map.name: Market the company and maintain client relationships
process_map.description: Business development managers meet owners and consultants, prepare qualifications brochures and award entries, and host client events to learn about upcoming projects early. Leads are logged in the CRM.

evidence.note: General industry practice.

process_map.name: Prepare and submit a stipulated price tender
process_map.description: Estimators take off quantities, price self-performed concrete and general conditions, issue trade packages, carry the best compliant trade prices in the last hours before close, and submit a sealed lump-sum bid with a bid bond. Addenda, late trade prices and scope gaps make the final day error-prone.

surge.cause: spring public tender season before and after the government fiscal year-end

evidence.note: Public owners release much of their capital work between February and May; estimate.
Bid volume is an estimate.

process_map.name: Solicit and level trade bids
process_map.description: For each bid or CM package, estimators send trade packages to prequalified subcontractors and suppliers, chase coverage, and level the quotes for scope so that the lowest compliant price is carried. Many trade prices arrive in the final hour, often with exclusions.
process_map.unit_of_work: one trade package on one bid

evidence.note: Estimate of 25-35 trade packages per bid.

process_map.name: Prepare a construction management, design-build or IPD proposal
process_map.description: For negotiated and best-value work the team writes a proposal with fee, general conditions, staffing, schedule and approach, and attends an interview. Design-build proposals also need a design team and a priced concept design.

process_map.name: Pursue a P3 project as construction partner
process_map.description: In a consortium with equity investors, lenders and a facility manager, the contractor leads design development and the construction price and schedule for a P3 bid that can take 12 to 18 months. The pursuit costs millions and depends on a partial stipend if lost.
process_map.unit_of_work: one P3 pursuit, from screening the opportunity to financial close or loss

evidence.note: Volume from gc-bd-p3-pursuit (2026-11-24): One to four new pursuits a year; with pursuits lasting 12 to 15 months this gives one to three pursuits running at once, which matches the organisation file's 1 to 3 pursuit-months a month.

process_map.name: Deliver preconstruction services under a CM agreement
process_map.description: Under a preconstruction agreement the contractor prices each design stage, reviews constructability, proposes value engineering, plans phasing and tenders trade packages before the construction phase is priced. Owners compare budgets against their funding approvals.
process_map.unit_of_work: one preconstruction engagement, from the signed preconstruction agreement to an agreed construction price

evidence.note: Volume from gc-bd-preconstruction-services (2026-11-24): One to two new engagements a month, each lasting about 8 to 14 months, gives 10 to 20 engagements running at once, which matches the organisation file's 10 to 22 project-months of preconstruction a month.

process_map.name: Manage design on design-build projects
process_map.description: The design manager runs the design consultants hired by the contractor, holds design reviews with the owner, tracks compliance with the owner's statement of requirements and releases packages for permit and construction.

process_map.name: Negotiate and execute the prime contract
process_map.description: After award the business development lead, the project manager and contracts counsel negotiate supplementary conditions, insurance, bonding and schedule, then sign the CCDC or P3 contract. Unacceptable risk terms can delay signing for weeks. About half of the 10 awards a month come from the bid and proposal processes (about 3 from stipulated bids at a 1-in-7 hit rate and about 2 from CM and design-build proposals); the rest are negotiated work for repeat clients, contract extensions and work orders under master service agreements, which skip formal bidding.

evidence.note: Revised 2026-11-24: The gc-01 author found that the bid processes yield about 5 awards a month, not 10. Bird secures work through bids or negotiation and books master service agreement work orders (src-bird-aif20), so the remainder is recorded as negotiated work.

process_map.name: Maintain the historical cost database
process_map.description: Estimators record final unit costs, productivity rates and trade prices from closed projects into the estimating database so that future bids price self-perform work realistically.

evidence.note: Common estimating practice.

process_map.name: Start up a project and turn it over from estimating
process_map.description: Estimating hands the project to the operations team in a turnover meeting; the project manager loads the budget by cost code, sets up the job in the ERP and project platform, assigns the team, and launches buyout, safety planning, permits and mobilization. Gaps between the bid and the contract surface here.

evidence.note: General contractor practice.

process_map.name: Mobilize the site
process_map.description: The superintendent plans site logistics, installs hoarding, trailers and temporary power and water, sets crane and hoist locations and arranges site access before trades arrive. Permits and utility locates often hold up the start.

evidence.note: General contractor practice.

process_map.name: Obtain permits, inspections and utility connections
process_map.description: The project team applies for building, demolition, road occupancy and hoarding permits, books municipal inspections and coordinates utility connections. Municipal review times and utility schedules sit outside the contractor's control.

evidence.note: Municipal approvals typical of Ontario projects.

process_map.name: Build and update the project schedule
process_map.description: Schedulers and superintendents build a baseline CPM schedule, update it monthly with site progress, analyse delays and issue look-ahead schedules for trades. Delay analysis supports extension of time requests.

evidence.note: Common CPM practice; CCDC contracts require a construction schedule.

process_map.name: Coordinate trades in the BIM model
process_map.description: On complex buildings such as hospitals, VDC coordinators combine trade models, run clash detection, and hold weekly coordination meetings until mechanical, electrical and structural routes fit. Unresolved clashes become RFIs.

evidence.note: Volume is an estimate.

process_map.name: Coordinate the site day to day
process_map.description: The superintendent runs the daily start-up, sequences trades, checks deliveries and manpower, walks the work, resolves conflicts and writes the daily report. Weather, late trades and missing information cause constant re-planning.

evidence.note: 220 projects x 21 working days.

process_map.name: Manage requests for information
process_map.description: Field engineers and trades raise questions about unclear or conflicting drawings; the project team writes the RFI in the project platform, sends it to the consultant, chases the answer and distributes it. Late answers stop work and many answers change scope.

evidence.note: Volume from gc-ops-rfi (2026-11-24): Navigant: 17.2 RFIs per $1 million of construction cost on $5M-$50M projects (src ascc). At about $1.5 billion of annual construction revenue this gives about 2,150 RFIs a month; low and high allow for revenue of $1.2B to $2.0B and for institutional work, which tends to run higher. The organisation file's 3,300 a month (15 per project per month) is above this.

process_map.name: Manage shop drawings and submittals
process_map.description: Trades send shop drawings, product data and samples; the project team checks them against the specifications, stamps and forwards them to the consultant, tracks review times and releases approved items for fabrication. Long consultant reviews delay procurement of long-lead items.

evidence.note: Estimate of submittal counts per project.

process_map.name: Price and process owner changes
process_map.description: When the consultant issues a proposed change or a site condition changes the work, the project team gathers trade prices, prices self-perform work, submits a quotation, negotiates and either gets a change order or proceeds on a change directive. Disputed changes and slow approvals tie up cash.

evidence.note: Volume is an estimate.

process_map.name: Process subcontract change orders
process_map.description: Each owner change and many site instructions require pricing and issuing changes to the affected subcontracts, matched to the owner change so that cost and revenue stay aligned. Trade claims for extras not covered by an owner change are frequent.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Inspect and test the work
process_map.description: Field engineers and superintendents run quality checklists before covering work, book third-party testing of concrete and soils, and record non-conformances for correction. Failed tests can mean demolishing and redoing work.

evidence.note: Volume is an estimate.

process_map.name: Hold owner and consultant progress meetings
process_map.description: Every two weeks the project manager meets the owner and consultant to review schedule, changes, RFIs and submittals, and issues minutes. Decisions taken here release changes and payments.

evidence.note: Common practice.

process_map.name: Protect and heat the work in winter
process_map.description: From November to March the team plans enclosures, temporary heat and concrete protection so work can continue, orders heaters and fuel, and sends carpentry crews to build hoarding. Cold snaps force sudden extra heat and can stop pours.

evidence.note: Canadian winter weather; estimate.
Canadian winter construction practice.

process_map.name: Prepare the monthly progress draw
process_map.description: Each month the project manager values work done against the schedule of values, adds approved change orders, and the project accountant issues the proper invoice with the statutory declaration and WSIB clearance. The consultant certifies the amount and the 28-day prompt payment clock starts.

process_map.name: Prepare the monthly cost report and forecast
process_map.description: The project manager and project controls reconcile committed and actual cost by cost code, estimate cost to complete, and report margin fade or gain. These forecasts drive revenue recognition, so optimistic forecasts become write-downs later.

evidence.note: Percentage-of-completion accounting practice.

process_map.name: Commission building systems
process_map.description: Near completion, mechanical, electrical and controls trades start up and test systems with the commissioning agent and owner staff. Defects found here delay takeover, especially in hospitals.

process_map.name: Close deficiencies and reach substantial performance
process_map.description: The consultant issues deficiency lists, trades fix them, and the contractor applies for substantial performance or Ready-for-Takeover with occupancy, manuals and training. Publication of the certificate starts the lien and holdback periods.

surge.cause: summer handover rush for schools needed by Labour Day

evidence.note: School boards require occupancy before September; estimate.

process_map.name: Assemble closeout documents
process_map.description: Coordinators collect operation and maintenance manuals, as-built drawings, warranties and training records from every trade and hand them to the owner. Chasing trades for documents holds up the final holdback release.

process_map.name: Handle warranty claims
process_map.description: During the one-year warranty period owners report defects; the warranty coordinator assigns them to the responsible trade, follows up and records completion. Trades that have left the market leave the contractor to fix the defect itself.

evidence.note: Standard one-year warranty in CCDC contracts; volume estimated.

process_map.name: Close out the project financially
process_map.description: After takeover the team settles final accounts with trades and the owner, releases unused contingency, closes the job in the ERP and records lessons learned. Open claims can keep jobs open for years.

evidence.note: General practice.

process_map.name: Manage subcontractor performance and default
process_map.description: When a trade falls behind, lacks manpower or fails quality or safety checks, the project manager issues notices, supplements its work and, if needed, declares default and calls on its bond. Default is rare but expensive.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Report to the P3 consortium, lenders and certifier
process_map.description: On P3 projects the construction team reports monthly to Project Co, the lenders' technical advisor and the independent certifier on progress, schedule and quality, because payment comes at substantial completion. Missing milestones costs the consortium financing.

process_map.name: Plan and allocate self-perform crews
process_map.description: Each week the general foremen and the self-perform director match crew requests from projects against available foremen, trades and formwork, call extra trades from the union hall or lay them off. Pours compete for the same crews and weather shifts plans daily.

process_map.name: Form, place and finish concrete
process_map.description: Crews set forms and shoring, coordinate rebar and embedded services with trades, pass the pre-pour inspection, place concrete from trucks by pump or crane bucket and finish and cure it. Weather, late ready-mix trucks and failed inspections stretch pours.

surge.cause: construction season (May to October), when concrete, earthworks and exterior work peak

evidence.note: Seasonal pattern of Canadian concrete work; estimate.
Pour counts are an estimate.

process_map.name: Carry out carpentry and general labour works
process_map.description: Carpentry and labour crews install hoarding, doors and frames, blocking and rough carpentry, temporary protection and clean-up, filling gaps between trades. Much of this work is billed as general conditions, so crews are moved often between projects at short notice.

evidence.note: General contractor self-perform scope.

process_map.name: Record crew time and cost codes
process_map.description: Foremen record each worker's daily hours by cost code on paper or a tablet, general foremen approve them weekly, and payroll and cost reports use them. Wrong cost codes distort the cost forecast; late sheets delay payroll.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Dispatch equipment to sites
process_map.description: Superintendents request equipment; the yard coordinator assigns owned units or rents them, books trucks and tracks where each unit is so that internal rates can be charged. Units left idle on sites cost money.

surge.cause: construction season (May to October), when concrete, earthworks and exterior work peak

evidence.note: Estimate.
Estimate.

process_map.name: Maintain and inspect equipment
process_map.description: Mechanics carry out scheduled maintenance, annual crane and hoist inspections and breakdown repairs in the yards and on site. A broken crane stops a whole site.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Erect, operate and dismantle cranes
process_map.description: The equipment team plans tower crane erection and dismantle, mobile crane set-ups and critical lifts with an engineer, checks ground conditions, and assigns certified operators. Wind and permit windows decide the day.
process_map.unit_of_work: one crane set-up, critical lift or dismantle

evidence.note: Practice under provincial crane rules; estimate.

process_map.name: Manage the formwork and materials yard
process_map.description: Yard staff receive formwork and shoring back from sites, clean, repair and count it, and ship sets to the next project. Lost or damaged forms are charged to projects.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Plan site safety and file the notice of project
process_map.description: Before work starts the safety manager and superintendent prepare the site-specific safety plan, emergency plan and hazard register, file the notice of project with the ministry and set up the joint health and safety committee where required. The contractor is the constructor and carries the legal duties.

evidence.note: Constructor duties under provincial OHS law; CCDC GC 9.4.

process_map.name: Complete daily hazard assessments and toolbox talks
process_map.description: Every crew completes a field-level hazard assessment before starting work and the foreman holds a toolbox talk; the safety coordinator reviews the forms. Quality varies and copied forms are common.

evidence.note: Common practice under COR programs.

process_map.name: Inspect sites and run the safety committee
process_map.description: Safety coordinators and committee members inspect each site weekly, record unsafe conditions and follow up corrective actions with trades. Repeat findings lead to notices and removal of workers.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Report and investigate incidents
process_map.description: Injuries, near misses, property damage and spills are reported the same day, investigated for root cause, reported to the workers' compensation board and, for critical injuries, to the ministry, and injured workers return to modified work. Lost-time injuries affect bidding.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Respond to ministry inspections and orders
process_map.description: When a ministry inspector visits a site the superintendent and safety coordinator accompany them, and any orders are fixed and confirmed in writing. Stop-work orders halt work immediately.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Train and orient workers
process_map.description: New hires and trades get site orientation and required certifications such as working at heights, WHMIS and rigging, tracked in the training records. Spring hiring brings a rush of orientations.

evidence.note: Estimate.
Estimate.

process_map.name: Manage environmental compliance on sites
process_map.description: The environmental specialist sets erosion, dust, dewatering, spill and waste diversion plans, checks sites and reports spills. Excavated soil and contamination rules add cost and delay.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Maintain safety certification (COR)
process_map.description: Each year the safety program is audited against the Certificate of Recognition standard by internal and external auditors. Owners require COR to bid, so a failed audit would block the company from many public tenders; preparing evidence takes weeks.

evidence.note: COR is a common prequalification requirement in Canada.

process_map.name: Prequalify subcontractors
process_map.description: Analysts collect questionnaires, financials, insurance certificates, WSIB clearances and safety statistics from trades, set limits, and keep the approved list current. Expired insurance and clearance certificates are the usual gap.

evidence.note: Volume from gc-scm-subcontractor-prequal (2026-11-24): About 45 to 70 new firms a month (the organisation file's 40 to 90) plus annual renewals of an approved list of roughly 700 to 1,000 active trades; the renewal count is the author's estimate from about 3,000 active subcontracts.

process_map.name: Award subcontracts and purchase orders (buyout)
process_map.description: After award the project manager and subcontract administrator negotiate with the bidding trades, confirm scope, and issue subcontracts and purchase orders. Buyout savings or losses against the estimate set the project's early margin.

evidence.note: 25 trade packages per project; estimate.

process_map.name: Buy and expedite materials
process_map.description: Buyers issue purchase orders for self-perform materials such as ready-mix, rebar, lumber and consumables and for owner-direct long-lead items, expedite deliveries and match receipts. Long lead times and price escalation in 2021-22 made this harder.

surge.cause: construction season (May to October), when concrete, earthworks and exterior work peak

evidence.note: Estimate.
Estimate.

process_map.name: Set up and maintain vendors
process_map.description: Vendor requests are checked for tax numbers, banking details and duplicates and created in the ERP. Bank-detail changes are confirmed by phone because of fraud risk.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Process and pay subcontractor progress invoices
process_map.description: Subcontractors submit monthly progress invoices; the project manager approves the percentage complete, AP checks holdback, WSIB clearance and statutory declarations, and payment goes out within 7 days of receiving the owner's payment on Ontario contracts procured after 1 October 2019; older contracts and most work in other provinces pay when the owner pays. Disputed amounts need a notice of non-payment on time.

process_map.name: Process supplier and rental invoices
process_map.description: AP scans supplier, rental and ready-mix invoices, matches them to purchase orders and receipts, routes them to site for coding and pays them on terms. Missing receipts and wrong cost codes cause rework.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Collect owner payments
process_map.description: Billing specialists track certified draws against the 28-day deadline, chase late payments and notices of non-payment, apply receipts and flag disputed amounts for adjudication. Slow public owners stretch working capital.

process_map.name: Track and release holdback
process_map.description: Finance tracks the 10% holdback owed by owners and to trades, bills it after substantial performance or phased release, checks for liens after the lien period, and pays trades. Unresolved liens delay release.

evidence.note: Volume from gc-fin-holdback-release (2026-11-24): About 10 substantial performances a month (organisation file: 7-14 deficiency closeouts and about 10 project starts a month) plus about 6 phased or early trade releases; lower than the organisation file's 15-40.

process_map.name: Run weekly hourly payroll
process_map.description: Payroll loads approved timesheets, applies the rates, overtime and premiums of several collective agreements and provinces, pays workers weekly and remits union dues, benefits, pension and WCB premiums. Many agreements and late corrections make it error-prone.

evidence.note: Weekly pay is common for union construction trades.

process_map.name: Run salaried payroll
process_map.description: Payroll pays salaried staff every two weeks, applies new hires, changes and terminations from the HRIS, and remits source deductions. Mid-cycle changes and project bonus payments are the usual sources of corrections.

evidence.note: Standard practice.

process_map.name: Close the books each month
process_map.description: Finance closes job cost, posts accruals and equipment charges, recognises revenue from project cost forecasts by percentage of completion and reports results by region. Late forecasts and unapproved changes hold up the close.

evidence.note: Standard construction accounting.

process_map.name: Publish quarterly and annual financial reports
process_map.description: The reporting team prepares financial statements, MD&A, backlog disclosure and the annual information form, supports the auditors and files with securities regulators. Judgements on loss projects and claims get the most audit attention.

process_map.name: Obtain bid and performance bonds
process_map.description: The treasury manager requests bid bonds for tenders and performance and labour and material payment bonds after award, and reports financial results to the surety to keep the bonding line. Public contracts in Ontario require both bonds above a prescribed value.

process_map.name: Manage cash and the credit facility
process_map.description: Treasury prepares a weekly cash forecast, manages draws on the revolving credit facility and letters of credit, and monitors covenants. Slow owner payments and holdback build-up drive draws, and the surety watches working capital closely.

process_map.name: Prepare the annual budget
process_map.description: Finance builds the annual budget from backlog, expected awards, overhead and equipment capital, and executives approve it with the board. The budget depends on guessing which pending bids will be won and when they start.

evidence.note: Standard practice.

process_map.name: File tax returns
process_map.description: Finance files HST, payroll and corporate tax returns in each province, including provincial sales tax in some provinces. Self-assessed sales tax on materials used on site is a common audit finding.

evidence.note: Standard practice.

process_map.name: Hire trades through the union hall
process_map.description: When crew planning needs more trades, foremen or HR call the union hall for dispatch or name-hire members, collect documents and certifications, and send them to orientation. Shortages in peak season delay crews.

evidence.note: Estimate.
ICI union hiring practice in Ontario; estimate.

process_map.name: Lay off and recall trades
process_map.description: At the end of a scope, or as winter slows work, trades are laid off with records of employment and returned to the hall; recalls follow in spring.

evidence.note: Estimate.
Estimate.

process_map.name: Manage collective agreements and grievances
process_map.description: The labour relations manager administers collective agreements with the trades, handles grievances and jurisdiction disputes, and takes part in province-wide ICI bargaining through employer associations.

evidence.note: Ontario ICI bargaining practice.

process_map.name: Recruit salaried staff
process_map.description: Recruiters fill project manager, superintendent, engineer and office roles from postings and referrals, and onboard new hires. Competition for experienced site staff is strong, and offer timing must match project start dates that often slip.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Run performance reviews and compensation
process_map.description: Once a year managers rate staff, HR calibrates ratings and pay increases against the budget, and bonuses tied to project results are paid. Project staff spread across many sites make timely reviews hard to complete.

evidence.note: Standard practice.

process_map.name: Resolve IT tickets
process_map.description: Analysts handle password resets, device set-ups, software and access requests from offices and sites. Remote sites make device swaps slow, and site staff often call with urgent problems on the platform during working hours.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Connect new site offices
process_map.description: IT orders internet, sets up network equipment, printers and plotters in site trailers and removes them at closeout. Rural sites depend on cellular or satellite links.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Change the ERP and project platform
process_map.description: Business systems analysts configure the ERP and project platform for new cost codes, workflows and reports, test changes and release them. Changes are scheduled outside month-end close so that billing and payroll are not disrupted.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Review prime contract terms
process_map.description: Contracts counsel reviews supplementary conditions in tenders and draft contracts for liability, liquidated damages, consequential damages, indemnities and payment terms, and advises on exceptions. Review time is short because tender periods often allow only a few weeks.

process_map.name: Manage claims and disputes
process_map.description: The claims manager prepares delay and change claims with schedule analysis and cost records, negotiates with owners and runs mediation, arbitration or litigation. Large claims take years.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Handle liens and adjudication
process_map.description: Legal responds to liens registered by trades, vacates them by posting security, and starts or answers adjudications of payment disputes, which an adjudicator decides within 30 days. Liens must be preserved within 60 days.

evidence.note: Volume from gc-legal-lien-adjudication (2026-11-24): Author's estimate, below the organisation file's 4-8-14. Ontario-wide only 50 (fiscal 2021) and 121 (fiscal 2022) adjudications were started, of which about 16 and 39 were commercial, public buildings or industrial (src osler_odacc2, osler_odacc3), so this contractor is party to only a few a year; lien volume is set at about one a month per 40 to 50 active projects.

process_map.name: Run the insurance program and claims
process_map.description: The risk manager places project insurance (wrap-up, builder's risk), issues certificates to owners and manages claims for damage, theft and third-party injury. Every owner contract and many subcontracts need certificates naming additional insureds.

evidence.note: Estimate.

assumptions: The organisation is a composite: it has the delivery models, markets and Ontario head office of Bird Construction before its 2020 Stuart Olson acquisition, scaled to about $1.5B revenue and 2,800 employees. Industrial maintenance, mining and heavy civil work that Bird also does are left out because the brief is a buildings general contractor.

Bird's 2020 annual information form (src-bird-aif20) gives its staffing: about 880 salaried and 1,578 hourly employees at 31 December 2019, on 2019 revenue of $1,376.4 million. Office lists and self-perform shares remain tier C estimates.

Ontario's statutes and regulations (Construction Act, O. Reg. 213/91) could not be opened on ontario.ca or CanLII; their prompt payment, holdback, lien and adjudication rules are cited from law firm summaries (src6, src7) and are tier B.

Employees = about 1,536 salaried staff plus about 1,344 hourly union trades on average; hourly headcount swings from about 1,050 in winter to 1,700 in summer. Headcounts were first set at 2,800 and raised on 2026-11-24 to 2,880 to cover the work the workflows record. Bird's total at the end of 2019 (2,458 for $1.38 billion of revenue) scales to about 2,680 at this company's $1.5 billion, but Bird's split was about 36% salaried, against about half here.

Loaded cost per hour uses a 1.35 loading factor for salaried staff and about 1.6 for union trades (benefit, pension and training fund contributions); Job Bank 2024-25 wages were deflated about 12% to 2019-22.
Project staff roles are listed at the operations division level and deployed across the three regional site networks; regional headcounts show where they sit.
Process volumes are tier C estimates derived from about 220 active projects, 10 project starts a month and about 3,000 active subcontracts.
Shift pattern extended_hours on site roles reflects 10-hour days and Saturday work in the construction season; office roles have no shift pattern.
The 2019-2022 period includes COVID-19 site protocols that lowered productivity in 2020-2021 (src2) and material price escalation in 2021-2022; process volumes describe an ordinary year.

Superintendents, assistant superintendents and field engineers are sized at 180 productive hours a month (productive_hours_per_month): their paid time is nearly all on site, with 10-hour days and some Saturdays in season.
